\par However, since the representability cells are also isomorphisms, the
conditions required above uniquely determine each invertible cell
$\phi$ (as the composite of two representability cells). The case of
bicategories is similar. Thus the pseudo-morphisms are simply functors
of the underlying {implicit} structures, recovering the categories
\bBicat and $\mathbf{WDblCat}$ from \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{sec:twowords} and
\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{sec:shortcut}:
\par\begin{prop}If $X$ and $Y$ are bicategories, then every functor $F:X\to Y$ of
\emph{implicit} 2-categories has a unique structure of pseudo
$T_{2}^{\wk}$-morphism.
\par Similarly, if $X$ and $Y$ are doubly weak double categories, then every
functor $F:X\to Y$ of \emph{implicit} double categories has a unique
structure of pseudo $T_{\d{}}^{\wk}$-morphism.\qed\end{prop}
\par\begin{cor}The 2-monads $T_{2}^{\wk}$ on \ctword, and $T_{\d{}}^{\wk}$ on \cDblWord, are
pseudo-idempotent. Therefore, an icon between bicategories or
doubly weak double categories is nothing more than an icon between
their underlying implicit 2-categories or implicit double
categories.
\end{cor}
\@proof The first statement is by definition of ``pseudo-idempotent''.
The second follows from~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{kl:property-like}{}{}, Proposition 6.7]}.
\qed\end@proof
\par\begin{rmk}In particular, every lax or colax $T_{2}^{\wk}$- or
$T_{\d{}}^{\wk}$-morphism is automatically pseudo. We could obtain
nontrivial notions of lax and colax functors by using the
alternative base 2-category suggested in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{rmk:cptd-bigon}.
\end{rmk}
\par\begin{rmk}The same arguments apply for the 2-monads whose algebras are strict
2-categories, strict double categories, and pseudo double categories.
In the fully strict case it is also sensible to consider \emph{pseudo
algebras}; these yield ``unbiased'' bicategories and a similar
notion of ``unbiased doubly weak double category''. General 2-monadic
coherence techniques as
in~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{power:coherence,lack:codescent-coh,shulman:psalg}{}{}]} can be
adapted to show that every such unbiased structure is equivalent to a
strict one.
\end{rmk}
\par We end this section by characterizing the relevant equivalences more
explicitly, and proving a coherence theorem for (biased) doubly weak
double categories.
\par\begin{lem}A functor of {{implicit} double categories} $F\colon\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{D}$ is an
equivalence in the 2-category \cDblWord if and only if it is
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@bijective on 0-cells,
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@locally essentially surjective on horizontal and vertical
1-cells, and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@bijective on 2-cells per boundary of 1-cells in $\mathbf{C}$.
\end{itemize}Therefore, a functor of doubly weak double categories is an
equivalence in the 2-category \cWDblCat if and only if it satisfies
these same conditions.
\end{lem}
\@proof Suppose $F$ is an equivalence, so there exists
$G\colon\mathbf{D}\to\mathbf{C}$ with invertible icons
$1_{\mathbf{C}}\cong G\circ F$ and $1_{\mathbf{D}}\cong F\circ G$. For
these icons to exist forces $F$ and $G$ to be inverse on 0-cells. We
also have that $F$ is surjective on isomorphism classes of 1-cells,
since $g\cong FGg$ for any 1-cell $g$ in $\mathbf{D}$. Finally, any
2-cell $\alpha$ is related to $FG\alpha$ by composing with
invertible icon components, so $FG$ is bijective on 2-cells per
boundary of 1-cells; likewise so is $GF$, and therefore so
must be $F$ and $G$.
\par Conversely, suppose $F$ satisfies the conditions above. We
nonconstructively define a functor $G\colon\mathbf{D}\to\mathbf{C}$. On 0-cells $G$ is inverse to $F$. For each 1-cell $g$ in
$\mathbf{D}$, we pick a 1-cell $Gg$ in $\mathbf{C}$ with an isomorphism
$g\cong FGg$. Now to define $G$ on a 2-cell in $\mathbf{D}$, we
compose on all sides with these chosen isomorphisms or their
inverses, then apply the inverse of the bijection on 2-cells given
by $F$. Functoriality of $G$ so defined follows from functoriality
of $F$, and we have an invertible icon $1_{\mathbf{D}}\cong F\circ G$
by construction. To define the icon $1_{\mathbf{C}}\cong G\circ F$ at a
1-cell $f$ in $\mathbf{C}$, we take the chosen isomorphism in $\mathbf{D}$
at $Ff$, then apply the inverse of the bijection on 2-cells given by
$F$. Naturality of this icon also follows from functoriality of $F$.
\qed\end@proof
\par\par\par\begin{prop}Every doubly weak double category is equivalent to a strict one.
\end{prop}
\@proof A doubly weak double category is defined as a representable
{{implicit} double category}, and {an} {{implicit} double category} is in turn defined as a
strict double category with free 1-cells. Hence every doubly weak
double category has an associated strict double category (the path
double category), its ``strictification''.
On the other hand, in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{cor:strict-double}, we saw that strict
double categories in the usual sense are identified with doubly weak
double categories that happen to be strict. Thus the strictification
of a doubly weak double category $\mathbf{C}$ determines another doubly
weak double category $\st\mathbf{C}$, which is strict. We will show
that $\mathbf{C}$ and $\st\mathbf{C}$ are equivalent {{implicit} double categories}.
\par Under the correspondence of \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{prop:main}, we obtain the
following description of $\st\mathbf{C}$: 0-cells in $\st\mathbf{C}$ are
0-cells in $\mathbf{C}$, horizontal or vertical 1-cells in
$\st\mathbf{C}$ are \emph{paths} of horizontal or vertical 1-cells in
$\mathbf{C}$, and a 2-cell in $\st\mathbf{C}$ (bordered by paths of
paths) is a 2-cell in $\mathbf{C}$ (bordered by the concatenations).
\par There is an evident functor $F\colon\mathbf{C}\to\st\mathbf{C}$
sending 1-cells to corresponding length 1 paths. This $F$ is clearly
bijective on 0-cells and bijective on 2-cells per boundary of
1-cells in $\mathbf{C}$. Moreover, $F$ is surjective on isomorphism
classes of 1-cells, since each 1-cell in $\st\mathbf{C}$ (a path in
$\mathbf{C}$) is isomorphic to a 1-cell in the image of $F$ (a length 1
path, a composite of the path in $\mathbf{C}$). Hence $F$ is an
equivalence by \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:equivalence}. (Moreover an equivalence in
the other direction can be constructed explicitly by choosing a
preferred way of associating compositions of paths.)
\qed\end@proof
\par
\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Double bicategories}
\par Our last goal in this paper is to give finite axiomatizations of
doubly weak double categories. There are actually many such
definitions, and we struggled with choosing which ones to present in
detail. In this section we give a definition that clarifies the
relationship to Verity's double bicategories (and \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{defn:tidier}
reduces it to a definition only involving cells of \emph{square}
shape); in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{sec:cubical} we give a definition that clarifies the
relationship to Garner's cubical bicategories; and finally in
\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{sec:finax} we give a monadic presentation using only finitely
many of the shapes of a double computad.
\par A {double graph with bigons} is a double computad whose only
2-cells are squares, horizontal bigons, and vertical bigons:

$factorsthrough\mathbf{BiDblGph}.\par Wenowrecallthedefinitionofdoublebicategory,writingoutalltheoperationsexplicitlyforreference.\par\begin{defn}A {double bicategory} consists of:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@A double graph with bigons. (That is, collections of 0-cells,
horizontal and vertical 1-cells, and horizontal bigon 2-cells,
vertical bigon 2-cells, and square 2-cells, related appropriately by
various source and target maps.)
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@The operations of a bicategory on the horizontal 1-cells and
bigons. Likewise, the operations of a bicategory on the vertical
1-cells and bigons.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@A top bigon-on-square action operation sending compatible
pairs of horizontal bigons and squares (where the bottom 1-cell of
the bigon is the same as the top 1-cell of the square) to squares.

\par Likewise, a vertical composition operation for squares.
\end{itemize}Furthermore, the following laws hold:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@Appropriate source and target laws for all ways of composing
bigons and squares.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@The laws of a bicategory for horizontal 1-cells and bigons, and
likewise for vertical 1-cells and bigons.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Identity, associativity, and mutual commutativity laws making
the left, right, top, and bottom bigon-on-square operations into
four compatible actions.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For any vertical bigon $\beta$, the identity square
commutativity law
$$\beta 1=1\beta$$(where the left hand side is the left action of $\beta$ on the
identity square of its codomain, and the right hand side is the
right action of $\beta$ on the identity square of its domain).
\par Likewise, the analogous identity square commutativity law for
horizontal bigons.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For any compatible horizontal string consisting of a vertical
bigon $\beta$ sandwiched between two squares $\zeta,\xi$,
the associativity law
$$(\zeta\beta)\xi=\zeta(\beta\xi).$$Likewise, the analogous vertical sandwiching associativity law.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For any compatible horizontal string consisting of a vertical
bigon $\beta$ to the left of two squares $\zeta,\xi$, the
associativity law
$$(\beta\zeta)\xi=\beta(\zeta\xi).$$Likewise, the analogous horizontal associativity law on the right,
and the analogous vertical associativity laws on the top and bottom.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@An interchange law that says the two possible ways of composing
two horizontal bigons side by side atop two horizontally adjacent
squares are equal.

\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@The interchange laws for squares as in a double category.
\par Specifically, the identity compatibility law states that vertical
identity squares on horizontal identity 1-cells agree with
horizontal identity squares on vertical 1-cells; the identity
interchange laws state that horizontal compositions of vertical
identity squares are vertical identity squares and vice versa; and
the square composition interchange law states that the two
possible ways of composing a two by two grid of compatible squares
are equal.
\end{itemize}\end{defn}\par Wewillshowthatdoublyweakdoublecategoriesareequivalenttodoublebicategoriessatisfyinganextra``tidiness^{\prime\prime}condition.\par\begin{defn}A {tidy double bicategory} is a double bicategory in which
the canonical map that sends \emph{2-cells in the horizontal
bicategory} to \emph{squares whose vertical source and target are
identities} is bijective

\end{center}Hence$\mathcal{C}_{M}$cannotarisefromanydoublyweakdoublecategory.\qed\end@proof\par\begin{rmk}Given \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:veritymonad}, the functor $\bWDblCatst\to\bDblBicatst$
is the canonical comparison functor to the category of algebras for
the induced monad on $\mathbf{BiDblGph}$. When such a comparison functor is fully faithful
(as it is in this case, by \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{cor:fftidy}), the right adjoint
forgetful functor (here $\bWDblCatst\to\mathbf{BiDblGph}$) is said to be
\emph{of descent type}~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bw:ttt}{}{}]} or
\emph{premonadic}~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{tholen:thesis}{}{}]}. There are many other
equivalent characterizations of this property, which are summarized
in~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{finitary-monads}{}{}, Theorem 2.4]}; perhaps the most
interesting is that \emph{every doubly weak double category has a
canonical presentation as a coequalizer of maps between doubly
weak double categories that are freely generated by double graphs
with bigons.}
\end{rmk}\par Thedefinitionoftidydoublebicategoryisconvenientbecauseitisfinite.However,itstillcontainsredundanciesthatcanbeeliminated.Ifwepareitdowntothebones,weobtainourmostconcisedefinitionofdoublyweakdoublecategory.\par\par\par\par\par\par\begin{prop}A doubly weak double category amounts to:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@a double graph,
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@horizontal and vertical 1-cell composition and identity operations (as in a double category),
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@horizontal and vertical square composition and identity operations (as in a double category), and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@horizontal and vertical associator and unitor squares (and their putative inverses) with identity 1-cells as their vertical and horizontal boundaries, respectively,

0-cells be points of $X$, the 1-cells be continuous paths
$p:[0,1]\to X$, and the 2-cells be homotopy classes of continuous
maps $[0,1]\times[0,1]\to X$ rel their boundaries. We take the
composition operations on these data to be the usual ones, and the
associator and unitor squares to be the usual reparametrizing
homotopies. It is then straightforward to verify the axioms.
\end{eg}\par Wewillalsoseeaworkedexampleputtingthisdefinitiontouseinthenextsection.\par\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Cubical bicategories}
\par Next, we compare our definition of doubly weak double category with
Garner's definition of cubical bicategory, which he described as
follows~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{garner:cubical-bicats}{}{}]}:
\begin{quote}\small Definition. A cubical bicategory is given by sets of objects, of
vertical arrows, of horizontal arrows and of squares, satisfying the
obvious source and target criteria, together with operations of
identity and binary composition for vertical and horizontal arrows,
satisfying no laws at all; and finally, for every
$n\mathord{\times}m$ grid of squares (where possibly $n$ or $m$
are zero), and every way of composing up the horizontal and vertical
boundaries using the nullary and binary compositions, a composite
square with those boundaries. The coherence axioms which this
structure must satisfy say that any two ways of composing up a
diagram of squares must give the same answer.
\end{quote}
\par Just like Verity's definition, Garner's definition can be derived from
ours by ignoring some of the structure of a double computad. Recall
that $\mathbf{DblGph}$ denotes the category of double graphs.
\par\begin{lem}The algebras of the monad on $\mathbf{DblGph}$ induced by the forgetful
functor $\bWDblCatst\to\mathbf{DblGph}$ are precisely Garner's cubical
bicategories.
\end{lem}
\@proof Garner's definition is obtained from the characterization in
\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{cor:freedescription} of the free doubly weak double category
on a double computad, specialized to the case of double graphs. (The
2-cells in free \emph{strict} double categories on double graphs are
given by grids of squares; this is well-known and also follows as a
special case of the description of free strict double categories in
the proof of \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:veritymonad}.)
\qed\end@proof
\par\begin{prop}The forgetful functor $\bWDblCatst\to\mathbf{DblGph}$ is not
monadic. (That is to say, doubly weak double categories are distinct
from cubical bicategories.)
\end{prop}
\@proof By \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:garnermonad}, it suffices to exhibit a cubical
bicategory that does not arise from any doubly weak double category.
In a doubly weak double category, there is a bijection between
2-cells of shapes

We now construct a cubical bicategory without this property. Given
any commutative monoid $M$ with identity $0_{M}$, let the cubical
bicategory $\mathbf{C}_{M}$ have one 0-cell, and let the horizontal and
vertical 1-cells both be freely generated, i.e.\ given by bracketed
strings of $1$. Let there be one 2-cell bordered on all sides by
$1$, which we label $0_{M}$

Hence $\mathbf{C}_{M}$ cannot arise from any doubly weak double category.
\qed\end@proof
\par However, \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:garnermonad} does also give us:
\par\begin{cor}There is a canonical functor from doubly weak double categories to cubical bicategories.
\end{cor}
\@proof This is the standard comparison functor from the domain of any right
adjoint to the category of algebras for the monad induced by the
adjunction.
\qed\end@proof
\par We now show that, as was the case for double bicategories, this
comparison functor is fully faithful, and we characterize the
image. (It is possible to quickly see that the comparison functor is
fully faithful using \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{defn:tidier}, but it will take us some
additional work to establish the following simple characterization of
the image.)
\par\begin{defn}A {tidy cubical bicategory} is a cubical bicategory such that
the canonical map induced by composing with an identity square (in
any of the four directions)

\end{defn}
\par\begin{prop}The comparison functor of \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{cor:cubical-cmp} is an equivalence
onto the subcategory of tidy cubical bicategories.
\end{prop}
\@proof Suppose given a tidy cubical bicategory.
We will construct a tidy double bicategory using the squares-only
definition from \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{defn:tidier}. That is, we require a double
graph equipped with binary composition and identity operations, such
that the canonical maps induced by composing with identities are
bijections per boundary, and the squares and ``bigons'' (squares
bordered appropriately by identities) with the induced operations
have the structure of a double bicategory.
\par Any cubical bicategory has an underlying double graph with binary
composition operations and identities (among other more general
composition operations). In particular, an identity square for (say)
vertical composition is obtained by composing a $0\times 1$ grid
using single identity 1-cells as the composites of the nullary left
and right boundaries. A \emph{tidy} cubical bicategory moreover by
definition has the same identity square cancellation condition of
\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{defn:tidier}.
\par As in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{defn:tidier}, we define horizontal (vertical) bigons to
be squares bordered by vertical (horizontal) identity 1-cells, and
we define the bigon-on-square and bigon-on-bigon composition
operations of a double bicategory by composing squares then applying
the given identity square cancellation bijection. We show this again
here for convenience:
$$\hbox to44.22pt{\vbox to74.92pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 22.37444pt\lower-36.78017pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

those to be the top and bottom composites for this grid, use single
identity 1-cells as the composites of the nullary left and right
boundaries, and obtain a coherence 2-cell. We will write all of
these coherence 2-cells as ``$\choseniso$'', save for the identity
squares written as ``$1$'' (which, observe, are a special case

\par Two formal composites, i.e.\ squares in a free cubical bicategory,
constructed from the same grid of squares are equal if and only if
they have the same boundary. (By definition, the 2-cells in a free
cubical bicategory on a double graph are compatible grids of squares
with bracketed boundaries.) In particular, any formal composite
featuring only coherence cells is itself a coherence cell, since
there is at most one formal composite with any given boundary
featuring \emph{no} squares.
\par We next verify the double bicategory laws. The double-categorical
interchange laws are automatic from the cubical bicategory
structure.
To show the remaining laws, note that in a \emph{tidy} cubical
bicategory, we have cancellation with respect to composing with
identities. Therefore one strategy to show an equation between two
squares is to compose both of them with identities and then to
express the resulting two squares as formal composites derived from
the same grid. (Then since we know these squares must be equal, by
cancellation the original squares are equal.)
\par Let us start with the unitor naturality laws. We must show that the
following compositions with coherence bigons are equal:

\par Moreover, we observe that the processes of translation between tidy
double bicategories and tidy cubical bicategories are inverse. It is
clear that a tidy double bicategory is recovered from the cubical
bicategory structure of its underlying doubly weak double category,
since all the data of \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{defn:tidier} are included in the
structure. Conversely, all the structure of a tidy cubical
bicategory is determined by the underlying tidy double category
structure, since an arbitrary grid composition operation is obtained
by binarily composing the grid and acting with coherence isomorphism
bigons to rebracket the boundary as desired.
\qed\end@proof
\par\begin{cor}The forgetful functor from doubly weak double categories to
cubical bicategories is fully faithful.\qed\end{cor}
\par\begin{cor}The forgetful functor $\bWDblCatst\to\mathbf{DblGph}$ is faithful and
conservative.\qed\end{cor}
\par Thus we can still regard a doubly weak double category as
``structure'' on an underlying double graph, though that structure is
not monadic.
\par\begin{rmk}Similarly to \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{rmk:premonadic}, \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{thm:cub-ff}
says that the forgetful functor $\mathbf{WDblCat}\to\mathbf{DblGph}$ is \emph{of
descent type} or \emph{premonadic}, and this implies that
\emph{every doubly weak double category has a canonical presentation
as a coequalizer of maps between doubly weak double categories that
are freely generated by double graphs}.
\end{rmk}
\par\par
\par\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{A finite axiomatization}
\par Tidy double bicategories do constitute a finite axiomatization of
doubly weak double categories: they are essentially algebraic
(presenting a finite limit theory) with finitely many types, finitely
many operations, and finitely many equations.
\par However, they do not share the good property of the infinitary
definition in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{sec:doublewords} of being presented as monadic
over a presheaf category in which \emph{pseudofunctors} can also be
represented as presheaf maps.
(A tidy double bicategory requires operations whose domains involve
identity 1-cells; however, identity 1-cells are not strictly preserved
by pseudofunctors.)
\par\par We now present another finitary definition, exhibiting doubly weak
double categories as monadic over a presheaf category with domain a
finite subcategory of that of double computads. The practical use of
this particular presentation is questionable, but the point is to
illustrate that something like it can be done. There are many axioms,
but most of them are adaptations of the axioms for double
bicategories.
\par A {monogon} in a double computad is a 2-cell of shape
$\ttw^{1,0}_{0,0}$, $\ttw^{0,1}_{0,0}$, $\ttw^{0,0}_{1,0}$, or $\ttw^{0,0}_{0,1}$.
A {double graph with monogons} is a double computad in which
all 2-cells are monogons or squares.
Let $\mathbf{MoDblGph}$ denote the category of
double graphs with monogons, a functor category whose domain is a
suitable full subcategory of $\lC_{\d{$}}:$$\vbox{\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\kern the full subcategory $\lE\hookrightarrow\lC_{\d{$}}including$\tz$,$$\theta$ $,$\tv$,and$$\ttw^{a,b}_{c,d}$$forall$a, b, c, d \leq 1$,sothat$[\lE, $\mathbf{Set}$ ]$givesthe``subunary^{\prime\prime}doublecomputads.Anaxiomatizationfordoublyweakdoublecategoriespresentingamonadon$[\lE, $\mathbf{Set}$ ]$couldpresumablybegiveninvolvingalargenumberofbinary2-cellcompositionoperations,removingtheneedfortheunusual4-aryoperationswehavegiven.Asamiddleground,onecouldalsogiveadefinitionusingmonogons,bigons,andsquares(involvingbothbinaryandternary2-cellcompositionoperations).\par Itistemptingtoconjecturethattheforgetfulfunctor$\bWDblCatst\to[\lE, $\mathbf{Set}$ ]$willbemonadicwhen$\lE$isanyfullsubcategoryof$\lC_\@text@daccent{$}includingthe0-cells,1-cells,monogons,andsquares.However,thisappearsnottobetrue:considerthecasewhere$\lE$consistsofonlytheseandthe2-cellshape$$\ttw^{2,0}_{0,0}$$.\end{rmk}\par\par\par\par\@@numbered@section{appendix}{toc}{Transformations and modifications}
\par In this section we discuss transformations and modifications of
{implicit} structures. We will see that when $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$
are {{implicit} 2-categories}, we obtain a {{implicit} 2-category} $\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$; in
the case $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are representable, this is the usual
bicategory of transformations and modifications of bicategories. More
than this, we will see that the \emph{lax and colax} transformations
of {{implicit} 2-categories} (resp.\ bicategories) assemble into a
\emph{{implicit} double category} (resp.\ \emph{doubly weak double category})
$\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$, providing a natural source of examples of
doubly weak double categories.
\par It is also true that when $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are {{implicit} double categories}
(resp.\ doubly weak double categories), we have a {{implicit} double category}
(resp.\ doubly weak double category) $\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$. However, we will focus on the 2-categorical case. This is
for reasons of space and also because we are unable to provide
motivation for studying transformations and modifications of doubly
weak double categories (we have no examples). Still, all of the
definitions in this section readily generalize to double-categorical
analogues.\par\par To figure out what the content of $\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ ought to
be, recall the defining property of an internal hom: it is universal
such that $\mathbf{C}\otimes\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ maps into
$\mathbf{D}$. However, this leaves us to wonder what the monoidal product
$\otimes$ ought to be. In ordinary 2-category theory, the relevant
monoidal product is the \emph{Gray tensor product}~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{gray:formal}{}{}]},
which composes 2-categories as if they were the homs in a semistrict
tricategory (so that closure for $\otimes$ induces a semistrict
tricategory of 2-categories).
\par This composition can be represented very cleanly using string diagrams, as described in~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{morehouse:two}{}{}]}.
Namely, a string diagram for $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ consists of a
string diagram for $\mathbf{C}$ superimposed over a string diagram for
$\mathbf{D}$.
For example, diagrams in
$\mathbf{C}\cong\Hom(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{C})$ can be composed with
diagrams in $\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ to yield diagrams in
$\mathbf{D}\cong\Hom(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{D})$:

\par The Gray tensor product is easy to express in terms of {implicit}
structures. Recall that a {shuffle} of linearly ordered sets
is a compatible linear order on their disjoint union.
\par\begin{defn}Let $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ be {{implicit} 2-categories}. The {Gray tensor product} of
$\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$, denoted $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$, is {an} {{implicit} 2-category} defined as
follows.
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@A 0-cell in $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ is a pair $(c,d)$ of a
0-cell $c$ in $\mathbf{C}$ and a 0-cell $d$ in $\mathbf{D}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@A 1-cell in $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ is \emph{either}
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@a pair
$(f,d)\colon(c,d)\to(c^{\prime},d)$ of a
1-cell $f\colon c\to c^{\prime}$ in $\mathbf{C}$ and a 1-cell $d$ in $\mathbf{D}$,
\emph{or}
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@a pair
$(c,g)\colon(c,d)\to(c,d^{\prime})$ of a
0-cell $c$ in $\mathbf{C}$ and a 1-cell $g\colon d\to d^{\prime}$ in $\mathbf{D}$.
\end{itemize}\par Equivalently, a path of 1-cells in $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ is a
\emph{shuffle} of a path of 1-cells in $\mathbf{C}$ and a path of
1-cells in $\mathbf{D}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@A 2-cell in $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$, with source and target
each a shuffle of a path in $\mathbf{C}$ and a path in $\mathbf{D}$, is
a pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ of a 2-cell $\alpha$ with the
source and target paths in $\mathbf{C}$ and a 2-cell $\beta$ with the
source and target paths in $\mathbf{D}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Composition of 2-cells is by composition in $\mathbf{C}$ and
$\mathbf{D}$.
\end{itemize}\end{defn}
\par We also define $\otimes$ on functors in the obvious way: if
$F\colon\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{D}$ and $G\colon\mathbf{C}^{\prime}\to\mathbf{D}^{\prime}$
are functors of {{implicit} 2-categories}, then $F\otimes G$ sends each cell called
$(x,y)$ to the cell called $(F(x),G(y))$ with
appropriate boundary.
\par\begin{rmk}This is the usual Gray tensor product of strict 2-categories,
specialized to {{implicit} 2-categories} (i.e.\ the Gray tensor product of
{{implicit} 2-categories} is the usual Gray tensor product of their path
2-categories). The description of the 2-cells given here follows
from the equivalence (see e.g.~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{gurski}{}{}, Corollary 3.22]})
between the Gray tensor product of 2-categories
$\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ and the cartesian product of 2-categories
$\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{D}$.
\end{rmk}
\par\begin{rmk}The above definition easily generalizes from a binary product to an
$n$-ary product, by replacing pairs and binary shuffles with $n$-tuples
and $n$-ary shuffles. In particular, observe that the empty Gray
tensor product defined in this way is {an} {{implicit} 2-category} with one
0-cell denoted $\grempty$ and no other non-identity cells.
\end{rmk}
\par\begin{prop}\tword is symmetric monoidal with respect to $\otimes$.
\end{prop}
\@proof[Sketch of proof]
Functoriality of $\otimes$ is immediate from the
defintion. Moreover, $\otimes$ is associative, unital
(\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{rmk:grayunit-two}), and symmetric up to coherent natural
isomorphism, by reparenthesizing and reordering the names of tuples.
\qed\end@proof
\par In \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{sec:twowords} we defined {an} {{implicit} 2-category} as a strict
2-category whose 1-cells are free, and we defined a functor of
{{implicit} 2-categories} as a 2-functor sending the generating 1-cells to
generating 1-cells. Now we define a {(lax or colax)
transformation} of {{implicit} 2-category} functors as a (lax or colax) natural
transformation of 2-functors whose components are generating 1-cells,
and we define a {modification} of {{implicit} 2-category} transformations as
a modification of (compositions of) these 2-category natural
transformations. We spell out the details below.
\par These definitions are appropriate in that they provide closure for the
Gray tensor product (to be shown in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{prop:gray-two}), and they
exactly give the usual notions of transformations and modifications in
bicategories, under the correspondence between representable
{{implicit} 2-categories} and bicategories (to be shown in
\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{prop:tranmain-two}).
\par\begin{defn}Let $F$ and $G$ be functors between {{implicit} 2-categories} $\mathbf{C}$ and
$\mathbf{D}$. A {colax transformation} $\sigma\colon F\to G$ consists of
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@for each 0-cell $A$ in $\mathbf{C}$, a 1-cell $\sigma_{A}$ in $\mathbf{D}$:

A {lax transformation} is defined dually, with
transformation component 1-cells at the northwest and southeast
corners of diagrams (diagrams mirrored).
\par When the $\sigma_{f}$ 2-cells are all invertible, we call $\sigma$
simply a {transformation}.

\par\begin{rmk}A transformation is both a colax transformation and a lax
transformation: given a colax transformation where the $\sigma_{f}$
2-cells are all invertible, the inverse 2-cells $\sigma_{f}^{-1}$ are
components of a lax transformation, and vice versa.

\par\par\par Just as a transformation is a morphism of functors, a modification is
a morphim of transformations. The most commonly seen definition of
modification goes between two (lax or colax) transformations. However,
there is a more general definition of modification that involves both
\emph{lax and colax} transformations. We actually get a (implicit)
\emph{double category} $\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ where the horizontal
arrows are lax transformations and the vertical arrows are colax
transformations.
\par\begin{defn}A {modification}

{\@@amsalign
}
\end{defn}
\par We define {horizontal compositions} and {vertical
compositions} of modifications
componentwise.
Likewise {horizontal (lax) identity} and
{vertical (colax) identity} modifications are identities
componentwise.
\par\begin{prop}Functors, lax and colax transformations, and modifications between
$\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ form {an} {{implicit} double category}
$\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ (via composition of modifications).
\end{prop}
\@proof The associativity, unit, and interchange laws are inherited from the
2-cells in $\mathbf{D}$.
\qed\end@proof
\par We denote by $\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ the {{implicit} 2-category} whose 0-cells are
functors $\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{D}$, 1-cells are \emph{transformations},
and 2-cells are modifications between these.
\par\begin{rmk}Given a colax transformation of {{implicit} 2-category} functors, if every
component 1-cell is a left adjoint, we obtain (upon choosing
adjunctions) a lax transformation in the other direction (where the
new component 2-cells are the \emph{mates} of the old ones).
A \emph{conjoint pair} in $\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ is such a pair
of colax and lax transformations, with component 1-cells in left and
right adjoint pairs.
\par On the other hand, as noted in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{rmk:lax-colax}, given a
colax transformation, if every component 2-cell is invertible, we
obtain a lax transformation in the same direction; this is the
content of a (non lax or colax) transformation. A \emph{companion
pair} in $\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ is (up to isomorphism) such a
transformation.
\par In general, {{implicit} 2-categories} may be identified with {{implicit} double categories} having
horizontal and vertical 1-cells in assigned companion pairs. (It is
the same as in the strict case; the translation from (implicit)
2-categories to such (implicit) double categories is the
``squares'' or ``quintets'' construction of \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{eg:bi-dbl}.)
The {{implicit} 2-category} $\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ is then embedded in
$\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ as the 1-cells with companions.
(The former is recovered up to equivalence from the latter through
the right adjoint to the quintets construction.)
\end{rmk}
\par It still remains to verify that $\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ in fact
provides an internal hom for the Gray tensor product. In other words,
$\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ is universal with a map
$\mathbf{C}\to\Hom(\mathbf{D},\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D})$:
\par\begin{prop}\tword is closed with respect to $\otimes$.
\par In particular, the Gray tensor product $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ is
the free {{implicit} 2-category} on the following data and laws:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@For every 0-cell $c$ of $\mathbf{C}$, there is a functor
$(c,-)\colon\mathbf{D}\to\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For every 1-cell $f\colon c\to d$ of $\mathbf{C}$,
there is a transformation $(f,1)\colon(c,-)\to(d,-)$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@For every 2-cell $\alpha$ of $\mathbf{C}$, there is a
modification $(\alpha,1)$ between the associated
transformations.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@Such modifications compose as in $\mathbf{C}$, with identities as
in $\mathbf{C}$.
\end{itemize}\end{prop}
\@proof Note first that the construction $\Hom(\mathbf{D},\mathbf{X})$ is
functorial in $\mathbf{X}$ (since functors, transformations,
modifications, and their compositions are shapes consisting of cells
and equations in $\mathbf{X}$), and a map from $\mathbf{C}$ into
$\Hom(\mathbf{D},\mathbf{X})$ is precisely the data in $\mathbf{X}$ as
described above.
\par It is easy to see that $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ contains such
data. Now suppose $\mathbf{X}$ also contains such data. We must check
that the induced map on the putative generating cells extends to a
unique functor $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}\to\mathbf{X}$.

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}$$\@@toccaption{{\lx@tag[ ]{{2}}{A generic 2-cell $(\alpha,\beta)$ in $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$.}}}\@@caption{{\lx@tag[. ]{{Figure 2}}{A generic 2-cell $(\alpha,\beta)$ in $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$.}}}
\end{figure}
\par All cells in $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$ are indeed compositions of
these generating cells: see \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{fig:grpair-two}. Here each 2-cell
written $(1,1)$, or ``shuffle'', may be composed in a
canonical way (up to associativity) from the transformation
component 2-cells
$(f,d),(c^{\prime},g)\to(c,g),(f,d^{\prime})$ or
their inverses, by constructing the induced permutation out of
transpositions. We accordingly extend the map
$\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}\to\mathbf{X}$ to arbitrary cells, sending
each 2-cell written as a composite of the generating 2-cells to the
corresponding composite in $\mathbf{X}$.
\par To show functoriality, consider 2-cells in the image of this
extended map $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}\to\mathbf{X}$, i.e.\ those
built as in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{fig:grpair-two}. Vertical composites reduce to the
desired form by transformation component 2-cells cancelling with
their inverses; horizontal composites are put into the desired form
using the naturality and modification laws.
\par It is then easy to see that the left adjoint acts as
$-\otimes\mathbf{D}$ on morphisms as well.
\par Alternatively, we could skip this argument by appealing to existing
knowledge about the Gray tensor product of 2-categories, of which
the Gray tensor product of {{implicit} 2-categories} may be viewed as a special
case; the Gray tensor product of strict 2-categories has a
presentation like the above since its internal homs are given by
2-functors, pseudonatural transformations, and modifications of
strict 2-categories.
\qed\end@proof
\par\begin{rmk}Replacing the transformations in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{prop:gray-two} with
\emph{(co)lax} transformations, we obtain the {(co)lax Gray
tensor product}~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{gray:formal}{}{}]} as the presented
structure. (The lax Gray tensor product is then the reverse of the
colax Gray tensor product.) However, it is perhaps less obvious
that this definition gives a (non-symmetric) monoidal product.
\end{rmk}

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}.$$Now the pushout of the unique functors $\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{D}_{1}$ and
$\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{D}_{2}$ is not preserved by $-\times\mathbf{I}$.
(Cartesian products in \tword are calculated using the essentially
algebraic definition of {{implicit} 2-categories} in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{sec:doublewords}; note
this does not agree with the cartesian product in \tcat.) Indeed,
this pushout has nontrivial composite 2-cells $\alpha$ with nullary
source and target, so its product with $\mathbf{I}$ likewise has
nontrivial 2-cells $(\alpha,1)$. On the other hand $\mathbf{D}_{1}$
and $\mathbf{D}_{2}$ have no nontrivial 2-cells with nullary source and
target, so the products with $\mathbf{I}$ are simply $\mathbf{I}$, as is
the pushout of these.
\end{rmk}
\par The next proposition implies in particular that if $\mathbf{C}$ and
$\mathbf{D}$ are bicategories, then $\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ is a doubly
weak double category.
\par\begin{prop}If $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are {{implicit} 2-categories} and $\mathbf{D}$ is
represented, then $\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$ (and hence in
particular $\Hom(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$) is represented.
\end{prop}

$\sigma\colon F\to G$ and $\rho\colon G\to H$ and identity
transformations (nullary composites) componentwise on 1-cells, and
with 2-cell components:

These are easily checked to be horizontal transformations. Moreover,

modifications. Lax transformations are similar.

\par\begin{rmk}The Gray tensor product of two representable {{implicit} 2-categories} is usually
\emph{not} representable: if $f\colon c\to c^{\prime}$ is an arrow in
$\mathbf{C}$ and $g\colon d\to d^{\prime}$ is an arrow in $\mathbf{D}$, there is
no composite 1-cell of the compatible $(f,d)$ and
$(c^{\prime},g)$ in $\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D}$.
\end{rmk}
\par\par\par Next we observe that our notions of transformation, modification, and
icon correspond to the usual notions for bicategories.
\par\par\begin{prop}Identifying represented {{implicit} 2-categories} and functors with bicategories
and pseudofunctors (\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{prop:main-two}) respects (co)lax
transformations, modifications, and icons, as well as their
composition.
\end{prop}

The axioms of a colax natural transformation then follow from
composition isomorphisms cancelling with their inverses and
applications of the colax transformation naturality axiom.
\par Conversely, suppose $\sigma$ is a colax natural transformation of
pseudofunctors. We define a colax transformation of the underlying
{{implicit} 2-category} functors as follows.
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@The component 1-cell at 0-cell $A$ is $\sigma_{A}$.
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@The component 2-cell is $\sigma_{f}$ converted to a
(2,2)-ary 2-cell:

for all chosen composition isomorphisms. We obtain the {{implicit} 2-category}
colax transformation naturality axiom for an arbitrary 2-cell
$\alpha$ by bracketing up its 1-cells and moving $\sigma$ across the
resulting bigon, as shown in \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{fig:i2ctna}.

These translation processes are clearly inverse. Moreover, it is
easy to see that identities, compositions, and whiskerings are sent
to identities, compositions, and whiskerings, as defined in
e.g.~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{johnson-yau}{}{}]}.
\par Our general notion of modification between lax and colax
transformations of {{implicit} 2-categories} corresponds to a notion for
bicategories defined in the same way, and it is easy to see that the
specialization to modifications between only lax or only colax
transformations (and their composition) coincides with the usual
definition, as in e.g.~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{johnson-yau}{}{}]}.

\par\begin{rmk}It is easy to generalize most of the results of this section to
double-categorical versions, with a few caveats. We refer the reader
to~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bohm:gray}{}{}]} for definitions of horizontal and vertical
pseudonatural transformations, modifications, and Gray tensor
products of strict double categories; see
also~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{morehouse:double}{}{}]} for definitions of horizontal and
vertical lax and colax transformations.
\par A maximally general definition of modification between both lax and
colax horizontal and vertical transformations of (implicit) double
categories can be formulated by placing transformation component
1-cells at all possible corners of the diagram:

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}$$\par One then expects to assemble some two-dimensional categorical
structure, analogous to $\Homl(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})$, in which 0-cells
are functors, 1-cells are lax and colax transformations, and 2-cells
are these generalized modifications. But here there are four
different sorts of 1-cells, apparently requiring an analogue of a
({implicit}) double category with octagon-shaped rather than
square 2-cells.
\end{rmk}
\par\begin{rmk}There is a relationship between double categories and (co)lax
transformations of 2-categories. Let $H\mathbf{C}$ denote the
vertically trivial (implicit) double category with horizontal
(implicit) 2-category $\mathbf{C}$, let $V\mathbf{D}$ denote the
horizontally trivial (implicit) double category with vertical
(implicit) 2-category $\mathbf{D}$, and let $Q\mathbf{X}$ denote the
(implicit) double category of ``quintets'' of (implicit)
2-category $\mathbf{X}$.
\par By comparing presentations, we can see that a (implicit)
2-category functor from the \emph{lax} Gray tensor product
(\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{rmk:laxgray-two}) of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ into $\mathbf{X}$
is the same as a (implicit) double category functor
$H\mathbf{C}\otimes V\mathbf{D}\to Q\mathbf{X}$. (Here the
double-categorical Gray tensor product $H\mathbf{C}\otimes V\mathbf{D}$
simply agrees with the cartesian product of strict double
categories, due to lack of nontrivial 1-cells of each type in some
factor. This is (the transpose of) the ``external product'' of
2-categories from~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{fiore-paoli-pronk}{}{}, Definition 2.6]}.) In
other words, the lax Gray tensor product of (implicit)
2-categories is given by $F(H(-)\otimes V(-))$, where $F$ is the
left adjoint to $Q$.
\par In particular, as can also be seen directly, lax and colax
transformations valued in a (implicit) 2-category can be described
as horizontal and vertical transformations valued in its associated
(implicit) double category.
\end{rmk}
